Getting Started with DataForSEO Google Organic SERP API: Parameters, Endpoints, and Response Structure – DataForSEO (https://dataforseo.com/help-center/getting-started-with-google-search-engine-api-documentation)
pages.text:
Getting Started with DataForSEO Google Organic SERP API: Parameters, Endpoints, and Response Structure – DataForSEO Help Center Search the Help Center Search Can’t find an answer? Get AI guidance on your account, billing, or implementation. AI Chat → Add as a preferred source on Google Getting Started with DataForSEO Google Organic SERP API: Parameters, Endpoints, and Response Structure SERP API Updated 18.11.2026 Table of Contents This getting-started guide walks developers through their first API call, from choosing an endpoint and constructing a request to authenticating and interpreting the JSON response. While our Google search engine API documentation provides a complete reference for all parameters and response fields, this guide focuses on what you need to get started. For more detailed instructions on specific steps, see our authentication guide with API key setup and code examples for credential configuration, or follow the step-by-step guide to scraping Google search results with Python for a Python-based walkthrough of the same workflow. If you need Google search results inside your product, whether that’s a rank tracker , a keyword research tool , or a competitive monitoring feature, you don’t have to build and maintain your own scraper to get them. That’s exactly what DataForSEO Google Organic SERP API is built for. It returns structured JSON from Google search, including organic and paid elements and SERP features, and delivers Live results back in about 6 seconds on average. The API documentation provides developers with all the details needed to understand, integrate, and use the Google search engine API effectively. Here we stick to the parts you need first, starting with how the endpoints are built. Endpoint structure and what the Google search engine API documentation covers Every endpoint in our Google Organic SERP API follows the same URL pattern, and it’s worth understanding its structure from the start to make integration easier: /v3/serp/google/organic/{mode}/{function} . These two placeholders correspond to two key values that build a complete endpoint. The mode controls how you get results. The Live mode returns data in real time in a single request (about 6 seconds on average), so it suits cases where you need to immediately display results to end users or perform a few on-demand checks. The Standard mode queues your task: you POST it, then collect it later by polling or through a pingback or postback URL. Standard mode runs at two priorities: normal (around 5 minutes) and high (around 1 minute), and it’s the lower-cost option for bulk search engine data collection. The function controls how much of the SERP data you get back. Regular returns the top organic, paid and featured snippet results without the full set of SERP features. Advanced returns a complete picture of the results page as structured items, including AI Overviews, knowledge panels, PAAs, and everything else. HTML returns the raw SERP page if you’d rather parse it yourself. To keep things straightforward, we’d point you to Live Google Organic SERP Advanced as the starting endpoint, because it gives you real-time delivery and the full SERP feature set. For complete field reference, you can turn to the Live Advanced endpoint documentation , and if you need the mode and function breakdown, you can learn more in the Google Organic SERP API overview . The SERP API Overview covers a wider set of search engines if you need more than Google. Once you’ve picked the endpoint, the next step is building the request payload for it. The request parameters that matter A request body is a JSON array of task objects, and most of what you’ll configure lives in three required fields plus a handful of optional ones. Here are the parameters that matter most when you’re getting started: Parameter Required? What it does keyword Yes The search query you want results for. location_code Yes* Location for which you want to collect search engine results (e.g. 2840 = United States). You can send location_name or location_coordinate instead. language_code Yes* Language for which you want to collect search engine results (e.g. en ). language_name works too. device Optional desktop or mobile . Defaults to desktop . os Optional OS for the chosen device: windows / macos for desktop , or ios / android for mobile . depth Optional Number of results to return. Default 10 . calculate_rectangles Optional Adds pixel-ranking coordinates for each element on the page. load_async_ai_overview Optional Set to true to obtain ai_overview items from SERPs even if they are loaded asynchronously. Note: this parameter adds one extra base price to the cost of the request. *One of the location field forms and one of the language field forms are required. Rankings and results displayed, including local packs, map results, ads, featured snippets, and even the set of organic URLs, can change depending on the searcher’s country, region, city, or ZIP-level location. If you don’t specify location_code , the API will use a default location, which may not match the market your product tracks or the location your client cares about. The same logic applies to language_code . It controls the language context of the SERP, including localized titles and descriptions, Google interface language, and in some cases the result set itself. For example, the query “best running shoes” can produce different results for users searching in the United States, Germany, or Spain, and those differences become even more visible when language is also changed. So, set location_code and language_code deliberately for every task. depth deserves a note on cost. Google Organic SERP endpoints are billed per 10 results, so a request with depth: 10 counts as one SERP and depth: 100 counts as ten. You’ll find the exact per-SERP figures on the Google Organic SERP pricing page . With the request shaped, you need API credentials to send it. Authentication and your first request Our API uses Basic HTTP authentication. You take the API login and password from your dashboard, encode them in Base64 as login:password , and send the result in the Authorization header. You can also copy a ready-made Base64-encoded value from the API Access section of the dashboard. The credentials stay visible there for 24 hours after account creation, and you can request them by email anytime later. Our Google SERP API authentication guide covers the rest, including no-code tools like Make and n8n and the five mistakes that cause most setup problems. The snippet below sends a single live request to the Google Organic Live Advanced endpoint and returns the JSON response. It’s the smallest working call and a useful baseline before you wrap it in a loop or a scheduled job. Because it’s plain cURL, you can reproduce it in any language. # Replace login:password with your credentials from the dashboard;
# the pair is base64-encoded inline for the Authorization header.
curl --location --request POST "https://api.dataforseo.com/v3/serp/google/organic/live/advanced" \
  --header "Authorization: Basic $(printf 'login:password' | base64)" \
  --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data-raw '[
    {
      "keyword": "best running shoes",
      "location_code": 2840,
      "language_code": "en",
      "device": "desktop",
      "load_async_ai_overview": true
    }
  ]' Endpoint used: Live Google Organic SERP Advanced. See the Live Advanced endpoint documentation for the full request field list and examples in PHP, Python, cSharp and more. If you work in Python, our Python guide to scraping Google search results makes the same first call with a ready-to-use script. One thing that trips people up early: the Live mode accepts only one task per request, even though Standard endpoints let you batch up to 100. If you need to run many keywords through Live, send them as separate calls within the rate limit (10,000 API calls per minute). For a fuller walkthrough of setting and collecting tasks, our guide on collecting SERP data with API covers both modes step by step. Go from API requests to automated workflows with our free SEO API Basics course. Take the course → Once the request returns, the next step is reading the response. The response structure and fields All API responses follow the same basic structure. The top-level object contains a tasks array. Each task includes a status_code (look for 20000 , meaning Ok), the cost of that task, and a result array. Inside each result is the metadata for the search ( keyword , location_code , language_code ) and an items array holding the SERP itself. Here’s a response for a single keyword, with some fields collapsed so the structure stays visible: {

} In practice, the items array is the most important and data-rich part. Each element has a type , and that’s how you tell SERP features apart from plain results. An organic item contains fields such as domain , title , url , breadcrumb , and description . AI Overviews, featured snippets, people-also-ask blocks, and local packs each have their own structure that you can explore in full from our Google Organic Live Advanced endpoint documentation . Two fields in SERP API responses handle ranking. The rank_group field is the position within results of the same type, while rank_absolute is the position across every element on the page. If an AI Overview sits above the first organic result, that organic result can have rank_group 1 and rank_absolute 2. For collecting AI Overview data specifically, check our guide on scraping Google AI Overviews . Once you know the shape of the response, a few habits help keep your integration smooth and stable. Implementation tips Here’s a quick list of best practices we’d recommend getting familiar with before you move from a first request to production: Test using the Sandbox first. Our Sandbox mirrors the production response structure and returns sample data, so you can build and validate your parser without spending on real calls. The Sandbox documentation lists everything you need to use it efficiently. Match the mode to your actual volume. At scale, the Standard queue costs less per SERP: $0.0006 versus $0.002 per Live depth-10 request. If you’re collecting thousands of keywords on a schedule, Standard with a postback URL is usually the better fit; reserve Live for on-demand lookups. Keep depth tight. Since billing is per 10 results, request only the depth your feature uses. Pulling 100 results when you display 10 multiplies the cost tenfold for data you discard. Plan your request volume. Whether you’re sending small, irregular batches or high-volume workloads, our guide to best practices for handling high-volume and low-volume SERP API requests explains how to structure and pace requests so they run efficiently rather than stacking up. Check unexpected results against a known-good request. If a call returns something you don’t expect, rebuild it in Postman alongside the narrated video in our blog post Making Your First Call to SERP API v3 , which sends Live and Standard requests step by step. If the Postman version works, look for the problem in your own code. For a quick recap before you build, the FAQ below answers the most common getting-started questions. Getting started with the SERP API: FAQ How do I get started with the Google SERP API? Copy your API login and password from the dashboard and send a POST request with a keyword , location_code , and language_code to the Live Google Organic SERP Advanced endpoint. The SERP comes back in the items array of the JSON response, where you handle each element by its type . Which SERP API endpoint should I start with? Start with Live Google Organic SERP Advanced: /v3/serp/google/organic/live/advanced . It returns results in a single request, in about 6 seconds on average, with the full set of SERP features, including AI Overviews, knowledge panels, and People Also Ask. Once your parser works, you can move scheduled bulk jobs to Standard mode. What’s the difference between Live and Standard endpoints? Live returns results in real time and takes one task per request, which suits on-demand lookups. Standard queues your task: you POST it, then collect the results by polling or through a pingback or postback URL. Expect around 5 minutes at normal priority and around 1 minute at high priority. Standard is the lower-cost option and takes up to 100 tasks per request, so it’s usually the better fit for bulk collection. How much does a Google SERP API request cost? Google Organic SERP requests are billed per SERP, meaning per 10 results, so depth: 100 costs ten times as much as depth: 10 . One SERP costs $0.0006 in the Standard queue and $0.002 in Live mode, and optional parameters such as load_async_ai_overview and calculate_rectangles add to the base price. The Google Organic SERP API pricing page lists current rates for each mode. Where do I find my API credentials? Your API login and password are in the API Access section of your dashboard. Our system generates the API password for you, and it’s different from the password you log in with. Our authentication guide shows how to encode them and add them to cURL, Make, n8n, or a Custom GPT. Wrapping up That covers the essentials of getting started. Our Google Organic SERP API gives you a set of clearly documented endpoints, fixed required parameters, straightforward Basic auth, and predictable JSON responses. These are the basics you need to pull structured Google search results into your product, without creating a custom scraping infrastructure or maintaining parsers every time Google changes the page markup. For pricing by mode and the other search engines you can query, see our Google SERP API page . Check the docs to make sure every parameter is set up correctly, explore the full list of available fields, get ready-to-use examples in PHP, Python, and other languages, and download our client libraries. pages.title: Common First Errors With DataForSEO API and How to Fix Them – DataForSEO (https://dataforseo.com/help-center/common-first-errors-with-dataforseo-api-and-how-to-fix-them)
pages.text:
Common First Errors With DataForSEO API and How to Fix Them – DataForSEO Help Center Search the Help Center Search Can’t find an answer? Get AI guidance on your account, billing, or implementation. AI Chat → Add as a preferred source on Google Common First Errors With DataForSEO API and How to Fix Them Getting Started Updated 18.11.2026 Table of Contents Running into errors is a normal part of working with any API, especially during the first integration. Most early errors with the DataForSEO API stem from predictable sources and causes, such as authentication issues, method selection, missing parameters, and usage limits. In this guide, we’ll cover the most common errors and suggest the best ways to deal with them. Important context: how to read DataForSEO status codes Our API servers return HTTP code 200 for almost every request, except for 401 (Unauthorized), 402 (Payment Required), 404 (Not Found), and 500 (Internal Server Error). So a 200 response doesn’t guarantee that you received data. The actual outcome is described in the status_code and status_message fields, which appear at two levels of the API response: Request-level codes (at the top of the response) indicate whether our system accepted and processed your API call. Task-level codes (within the tasks array) show the result of each task. Here is an example of a response from the SERP API that was successfully processed but had a task-level error: {
  "version": "0.1.20260717",
  "status_code": 20000,
  "status_message": "Ok.",
  "time": "22.3177 sec.",
  "cost": 0.002,
  "tasks_count": 1,
  "tasks_error": 0,
  "tasks": [
    {
      "id": "07231252-7652-0139-0000-301b3ccdda6f",
      "status_code": 40101,
      "status_message": "Internal SE Server Error.",
      "time": "22.2466 sec.",
      "cost": 0.002,
      "result_count": 0,
      "path": [
        "v3",
        "serp",
        "google",
        "organic",
        "live",
        "advanced"
      ],
      "data": {
        "api": "serp",
        "function": "live",
        "se": "google",
        "se_type": "organic",
        "keyword": "affordable car insurance policy",
        "device": "mobile",
        "os": "ios",
        "location_code": "2840",
        "language_code": "en",
        "load_async_ai_overview": true
      },
      "result": null
    }
  ]
} You can get a 20000 (Ok.) status code and message at the top level and an error inside a task, so always check both. Status codes starting with 2 mean success, 4 point to an issue with the request or account, and 5 indicate a problem on the API side or with a third-party source. You can find the full list of status codes and messages on the Errors page of our documentation. Authentication errors If you sent an API request and got a 401 HTTP code or a 40100 status_code , it means our system couldn’t match your credentials. In most cases, the cause is one of the following: Wrong API password. The DataForSEO API uses an API password, which is generated automatically at registration and is different from the one you use to log in to the dashboard. You can find it in the API Access tab of the dashboard. The API password is visible for 24 hours after registration, and then it can be sent by email. Wrong login. Your API login is the email address you used for registration. Credential encoding error. We use Basic authentication, so the Authorization header should contain Basic , a space, and the base64-encoded login:password string. An extra space or line break in the encoded string makes the request fail. However, a few other account-level errors can block your first requests: 40104: Your account isn’t verified yet. Complete the verification in the dashboard. 40207: Your IP address isn’t whitelisted. Add it in the API Access section ( learn more in this Help Center article ). 40200 or 40210: Your balance is too low to complete the request. Top up your account in the dashboard. For a full authentication walkthrough with code examples, see this guide . Data retrieval method issues: Standard vs Live Many of the DataForSEO APIs support two data retrieval methods: Live: You send a request and receive the results in the same response. Best choice for systems that require instant results. Standard: You set a task with the task_post endpoint and collect the results later with task_get . Use it if you don’t need instant results and want to process batch requests. Not every API supports both methods. For example, the DataForSEO Labs API and Backlinks API work in Live mode only. One of the common first errors is sending a request to a task_post endpoint and expecting data in the response. Instead, you get the 20100 (Task Created) status code and a task_id . This means the task has been accepted, and you need to make a separate task_get request to collect the results. Calling task_get too early is another common issue. If the task isn’t processed yet, you’ll receive status codes 40601 (Task Handed) or 40602 (Task In Queue) . These indicate that you should wait and request the results again. Additionally, if you get a 40401 (Task Not Found) error, check that the task ID, endpoint path, and hostname are correct. Specific endpoints, such as Google Organic SERP API Task POST , support the paid priority parameter. High priority puts your task in a priority queue, so you get results faster, but you still need task_get to collect them. If you need to retrieve results immediately, switch to the Live endpoint of the API you use (if available). Note that most Live endpoints accept only one task per request. Sending multiple tasks at once returns a 40000 error code (You can set only one task at a time). For more details, read the dedicated article on Standard and Live modes. Request body errors and missing required parameters Each endpoint has its own set of required parameters, so a request that works for one endpoint may be invalid on another. Before sending a request, check the required fields on the endpoint’s page in our docs. When a required parameter is missing or has an invalid value, you get the 40501 error code with the field name in the message, for example: Invalid Field: 'location_name' . Besides, across DataForSEO APIs and endpoints, required parameters may have different rules and value limitations. The most notable examples are the keyword and keywords fields . For example, in the Organic SERP API , a keyword can be up to 700 characters long and include search parameters that enable more granular search, but they multiply the cost of a request by 5. At the same time, in specific Business Data API endpoints, you can use the keyword field to pass cid and place_id values. There are also a few possible request body errors that may occur: 40503 (POST Data Is Invalid) : The request structure is invalid. Often, the body is sent as a single object instead of an array of task objects. 40506 (Unknown Fields in POST Data) : The body contains a field that the endpoint doesn’t support, usually due to a typo. 40006: A single POST request contains more than 100 tasks. To check a request before adding it to your code, you can run it in the DataForSEO API Playground or test for free with the Sandbox feature. Location and language errors Location and language parameters are probably the most frequent cause of request body errors. Most endpoints require one location parameter ( location_name or location_code , some endpoints also accept location_coordinate ) and one language parameter ( language_name or language_code ). The errors usually happen due to these reasons: The parameter is missing. The task returns Invalid Field: 'location_name' . The value has the wrong format. For example, London, UK returns the same error, while the accepted value is London,England,United Kingdom . Using location_code instead of a name can help to avoid such mistakes. The location isn’t supported by the specific API. Each API has its own list of available locations, so a location that works in the Google SERP API may not be available in the DataForSEO Labs API. To get valid values, use the locations and languages endpoints of the API you’re working with. For example, all supported locations and languages for the DataForSEO Labs API are available through the Location and Languages endpoint. Rate and concurrency limits If your integration sends many requests at once, you may reach one of our limits: 40202 (The rate limit per minute has been exceeded): The general limit is 10,000 requests per minute. 40209 (Too many simultaneous queries): You can send up to 30 simultaneous requests to specific APIs, such as the DataForSEO Labs API , Backlinks API , Content Analysis API , AI Optimization API , DataForSEO Trends API , and OnPage API . Some endpoints have lower limits. For example, Live Google Ads endpoints accept 12 requests per minute, so for larger volumes, use the Standard method. You can learn more about rate limits in this Help Center article . Wrap-up: “Making an error-free API call” checklist As you can see, most of the initial API errors are easy to resolve and avoid. Here’s a short checklist you can follow for making an error-free API request: Read our documentation and Help Center posts for the specific endpoints and APIs you want to use. Ensure that your DataForSEO API credentials are available and correct. Ensure that your account balance has sufficient funds to use our APIs. Check if the data retrieval method you chose meets your system requirements. Make sure the request body(ies) are valid and contain all required fields with correct values. Check whether your system meets our APIs’ rate and concurrency limits. Test your integration using the free Sandbox feature before working with real data. If something in your integration is still off or you need additional clarification, don’t hesitate to contact our 24/7 support team . New to SEO APIs? pages.title: How to Authenticate with DataForSEO Google Search SERP API: API Key Setup and Code Examples – DataForSEO (https://dataforseo.com/help-center/how-to-authenticate-with-dataforseo-google-search-serp-api-api-key-setup-and-code-examples)
pages.text:
How to Authenticate with DataForSEO Google Search SERP API: API Key Setup and Code Examples – DataForSEO Help Center Search the Help Center Search Can’t find an answer? Get AI guidance on your account, billing, or implementation. AI Chat → Add as a preferred source on Google How to Authenticate with DataForSEO Google Search SERP API: API Key Setup and Code Examples SERP API Updated 18.11.2026 Table of Contents Your DataForSEO API key is your API login and API password, joined as login:password and encoded in Base64. You’ll find both in the API Access tab of your dashboard, and the steps below show how to use them in Make, n8n, Custom GPTs, and cURL. The setup is simpler than the words around it suggest, even if API key, token, Basic Auth, and Base64 sound intimidating when you’re not a developer. Authentication is one of the easier parts of working with our APIs. You set up one credential pair, encode it once, and use it in whichever tool you’ve already got open: Make, n8n, Custom GPTs, scripts, AI agents. If you’re here for a Google Search API key example, you’re in the right place. This guide walks you through finding your credentials, encoding them, and getting them into that tool. Setting up Google Search API authentication: what you need to know When you’re searching for “Google Search API,” you’re probably looking for DataForSEO Google Organic SERP API . It’s a live source of Google search results, including featured snippets, AI Overviews, and other SERP features. We’ll use it as the example throughout this article, though DataForSEO authentication works the same across all our APIs. Set it up once, and you’re done. A quick glossary first, so the rest of the post reads cleanly. API login. A unique string our system generates to identify your account in API requests. On older accounts, the sign-up email may still function as the API login, however the owner can change it and switch to a generated one. API password. A separate password is automatically generated when you register an account with DataForSEO. It’s not the same as the password you use to log into the dashboard. This one authenticates your API requests. Basic Auth. Short for Basic Authentication. Instead of a single API key string, you send your API login and password with every request. It’s the simplest authentication pattern on the web, which is why we picked it. Base64. A format for safely passing characters like : and @ through HTTP headers. Base64 is encoding, not encryption — anyone with the encoded string can decode it, so treat it like a password. Header. The part of an HTTP request that carries metadata, including your credentials. Your encoded API login and password go in an Authorization header of every call. That’s the vocabulary out of the way. If you came here with one specific question, check the short answers below before the full setup. DataForSEO API key: FAQ How do I get my DataForSEO API key? Create a free account, log in, and open the API Access tab in the dashboard sidebar. Our system generates your API login and API password, and the two, encoded in Base64, are your API key. On older accounts, the login may still be your sign-up email. Jump to Step 1: get your API credentials Where do I find my API password? It’s in the API Access tab of your dashboard. Don’t confuse it with your account password: that one logs you into the dashboard, and only the API password works for API requests. Jump to Step 1: get your API credentials Why can’t I see my API password in the dashboard? The dashboard shows your API password for the first 24 hours after registration, then hides it for security reasons. After that, click Send by e-mail and we’ll resend it to the address on your account. Jump to Step 1: get your API credentials Is the DataForSEO API key the same as my login password? No. Your login password only gets you into the dashboard. The API key is built from a separate API password that our system generates for you, and mixing the two up is one of the usual reasons a request fails. Jump to Common authentication mistakes How do I encode my DataForSEO credentials with Base64? Join your login and API password with a colon ( login:password ) and encode that string with Base64. You can copy a ready-made encoded string from the API Access tab in the first 24 hours and request it by email after that, or make one yourself with a trusted online encoder or a one-line terminal command. Make and n8n do the encoding for you, so you can skip this step there. Jump to Step 2: encode your credentials with Base64 Here’s the full setup. Step 1 — Get your API credentials from the dashboard Create a free account on our website. New accounts get a $1 trial credit, and the SERP Google Organic Live Advanced endpoint costs $0.002 per call, so the trial covers around 500 live Google SERPs before you spend a cent. Enough room to set things up and run a few tests. Once you’re logged in, open the API Access tab in the dashboard sidebar. Two things most teams trip on here: Your API password is not the same as your account password. The account password gets you into the dashboard. The API password authenticates your API requests, and our system generates it automatically when you sign up. You don’t pick it. Your API password is visible for the first 24 hours after registration, then hidden for security reasons. If you missed the window, click Send by e-mail , and we’ll resend it to the address on your account. For a full walkthrough, see our help article on finding everything in the DataForSEO Dashboard . Now you have your API login and API password. On an older account, the login may still be the email you signed up with. The next step is to combine them into a format that an HTTP request can carry. Step 2 — Encode your Google Search API key (your DataForSEO credentials) with Base64 The fastest path is the dashboard itself. For the first 24 hours after registration, the API Access tab displays a ready-made, Base64-encoded string of your login:password . Copy it once, and you’re done. After 24 hours it’s hidden, for the same security reason as your API password, and you can request it by email instead. If you’d rather encode the credentials yourself, any of these three methods is just as quick. An online Base64 encoder. Paste your_api_login:your_api_password (with the colon between them) into any reputable encoder. Always use a trusted tool when handling a credential. A terminal command. On macOS or Linux: echo -n "your_api_login:your_api_password" | base64 . The -n flag matters; it strips the trailing newline that would otherwise cause the encoding to break. One line in your language of choice. Most languages have a built-in base64 library. We’ll show this in the cURL section below. Most no-code tools handle this step for you behind the scenes. You paste the raw login and password into two fields, and the tool encodes the result before sending the request. Worth saying twice: Base64 is encoding, not encryption. The encoded string is reversible by anyone who copies it, so don’t paste it into public chat channels, public repos, or shared docs. Treat it the way you’d treat a password. Step 3 — Plug the credentials into your environment The Basic Auth pattern works the same way in every environment. The credential doesn’t change. Only the field you paste it into does. Here’s what that looks like across the four most common paths. Make.com In your Make scenario, add an HTTP module and set the method to POST. Under Credentials , create a new Basic Auth connection. Paste your DataForSEO API login into Username and your API password into Password . Make handles Base64 encoding for you and adds the right Authorization header to every request. Save the connection and reuse it across scenarios. n8n Add an HTTP Request node to your workflow. Set the method to POST and paste the DataForSEO endpoint URL. Under Authentication , select Generic Credential Type , then choose Basic Auth in the Generic Auth Type dropdown. Enter your API login as the username and your API password as the password. n8n encodes Base64 for you. For a no-code workflow built on this pattern, see our walkthrough on automating keyword research with n8n and DataForSEO . Custom GPTs (ChatGPT Actions) In your Custom GPT’s Actions configuration, click Authentication , select API Key , and set Auth Type to Basic . In the API Key field, paste your Base64-encoded login:password string from Step 2. For the full walkthrough, including the OpenAPI schema, see our guide on connecting DataForSEO to ChatGPT . Direct API call with cURL If you’re sending the HTTP request yourself, from a script, a Google Apps Script in a Sheet, or a Claude Code workflow, the snippet below is the smallest working example. It hits our Google Organic Advanced SERP API endpoint and returns the top ten Google organic results along with any SERP features Google returned for the query. # Instead of 'login' and 'password' use your credentials
# from https://app.dataforseo.com/api-access
login="your_api_login"
password="your_api_password"
cred="$(printf "%s" "${login}:${password}" | base64)"

curl --location --request POST "https://api.dataforseo.com/v3/serp/google/organic/live/advanced" \
  --header "Authorization: Basic ${cred}" \
  --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data-raw '[
    {
      "keyword": "best serp api",
      "location_code": 2840,
      "language_code": "en"
    }
  ]' Endpoint used: api.dataforseo.com/v3/serp/google/organic/live/advanced . See the Live SERP API docs for the full parameter list. A successful call returns JSON structured like this: {
  "version": "0.1.20200214",
  "status_code": 20000,
  "status_message": "Ok.",
  "time": "7.7156 sec.",
  "cost": 0.002,
  "tasks_count": 1,
  "tasks_error": 0,
  "tasks": [
    {
      "id": "02171509-1535-0139-0000-fa36a0ff59c6",
      "status_code": 20000,
      "status_message": "Ok.",
      "cost": 0.002,
      "result_count": 1,
      "path": [ ... ],
      "data": { ... },
      "result": [
        {
          "keyword": "best serp api",
          "type": "organic",
          "se_domain": "google.com",
          "location_code": 2840,
          "language_code": "en",
          "check_url": "https://google.com/search?q=best+serp+api&...",
          "items_count": 100,
          "items": [ ... ]
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
} The top-level status_code: 20000 indicates that the request itself was accepted. The same code in the tasks array means your specific task succeeded. The cost field shows what you were charged, which is useful to watch while you’re testing. Common authentication mistakes (and how to fix them) Five issues cover most “why won’t it work” cases. Each one is fixable in under a minute. Using your account password instead of your API password. They look similar and live in the same dashboard, but only the API password authenticates API requests. Grab the right one from the API Access tab. Check the login as well: use the API login shown there, which may not be your sign-up email. Forgetting to Base64-encode the credentials. Sending raw login:password in the Authorization header returns a 401. The header value has to be Basic followed by a space and the encoded string. Putting credentials in the URL instead of the header. Our API rejects credentials passed as URL parameters. It’s a security choice, not a quirk. Send them in the Authorization header. Pasting the Base64 string into a public chat or repo. Base64 is encoding, not encryption. If a credential string has been exposed, regenerate your API password from the dashboard before continuing. Trial credit ran out before you noticed. The $1 trial covers about 500 SERP Live Advanced calls, but a loop with no rate limiting can burn through them in seconds. Top up from the Billing tab when you’re ready to go beyond testing. One last thing before you go live Authentication at DataForSEO uses a single credential pair: your API login plus your API password, encoded with Base64 and pasted into the auth field of your environment. The same credentials work across all DataForSEO APIs. Authentication is only the first step. Our Getting Started with the Google Organic SERP API guide picks up from here and walks you through endpoints, parameters, and your first request. Building in Python? Our guide to scraping Google search results with Python walks through the same first request with ready-to-use scripts. Before you start driving real traffic to the API, validate everything in our sandbox at zero cost. Just swap the hostname in your request from api.dataforseo.com to sandbox.dataforseo.com .
